headline: Parasitism is taking without giving—relationships where one benefits at another's expense
universal_truth: Not all relationships are mutual; some extract value without return; recognize the difference
fun_facts: Parasites are estimated to make up about half of all species on Earth
Some parasites can control their hosts' behavior—toxoplasma makes mice attracted to cats
Mistletoe is a parasitic plant that extracts nutrients from host trees
discussion_questions: How do you recognize when a relationship is extractive?
When might you be the parasite in a relationship?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: A tapeworm lives in your gut, eating your food, giving nothing back. A tick drinks your blood and leaves. Parasitism is the dark side of relationships—one organism benefits while the other pays. It's common, and not just in nature.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Parasitic relationships are everywhere—some obvious, some subtle. How do you recognize extraction versus mutual benefit?

options.text: Parasitism shows when one party consistently takes more than they give—energy, resources, or opportunities flow one direction without return
options.response: Yes. Track the flow: does value move both ways, or just one? Persistent imbalance signals parasitism. Occasional imbalance is normal; chronic imbalance is extraction.
Some are obvious, but the most successful parasites are subtle—you don't notice the drain...

q1.title: One-Way Flow
q1.script: In parasitism, value flows one direction. The parasite gains; the host loses. This differs from symbiosis where both gain. Direction of value flow reveals relationship type.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "One-Way Flow"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Subtle Extraction
q2.script: The best parasites aren't obvious—they extract just enough to benefit without killing the host. Some human relationships work the same way: slow drains that persist unnoticed.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Self-Audit
q3.script: You might be a parasite in some relationships—taking more than you give. Honest assessment prevents you from damaging relationships through one-sided extraction.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Not all relationships are mutual. Some extract value without return. Recognize the difference—and avoid being on either end.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 253. Tomorrow, we'll explore nature's cleanup crew—decomposers. Until then, audit one relationship for balance.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Balance Check - Give and Take Audit
growTrack.activity: Pick a relationship—personal or professional. Track what flows each way: energy, support, resources, opportunities. Is it balanced? If not, is that temporary or chronic? Address chronic imbalances before they drain you—or before you drain others.
